infotexts.entitydescription.oh_42_wh_c1: Issued from the ckl works in mid-1944, this size 64 shell carries the lot number 2979. Its Normandy camouflage was brushed on hastily, earthy greens and browns breaking up the outline beneath the hedgerows. Mud still clings in the rim’s recesses, as if set down in a foxhole after a summer storm. Some say it was left where its wearer fell, the liner stiffened by time, the steel carrying the silence of the bocage where battles raged and ended in whispers.
infotexts.entityname.oh_42_wh_sd1: Stahlhelm M42 (Heer) — single decal — ET64 lot 3119
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_42_wh_sd1: Stamped ET64 with lot number 3119, this helmet followed the later-war pattern of single-decal issue. The rough-textured paint has dulled to a matte tone, broken only by the army shield applied neatly to the left side. Its chin strap and liner remain intact, the leather drawn tight, pins unmoved since the factory. A piece that speaks less of camouflage and more of regulation — carried as issued, with its insignia still proud against the steel.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_42_ls_bd1: The bead along the skirt gives it away — a strengthened run turned aside from field issue and sent to the Luftschutz. This EF shell, size 66, carries the civil decal over rough paint, its edge rubbed smooth where fingers found the brim in dark stairwells. People remember sirens and cellar doors; the helmet remembers dust, broken glass, and the quick breath before the all-clear. A practical piece, worn hard in the nights when fires walked the rooftops.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_42_ls_bd2: The bead rolled into the skirt marks a different duty—steel set aside for the Luftschutz. This hkp shell, size 64, lot 1554, carries a civic badge over rough wartime paint; the strap’s hard sheen and the dry creak of the liner hint at long, anxious nights. It remembers stairwells and blackout curtains, the dust under cellar steps, and the hush between siren notes when a city counted breaths in the dark.
infotexts.entitydescription.ww2_stahlhelm_m42_base: A late-issue M42 from the ckl works, size 64, lot 3698. The paint lies flat and unadorned, a field finish without heraldry. Its rim shows a bright line where it was gripped again and again, the inside still holding the smell of old leather. Honest steel, carried by men in the last years of the war, marked more by wear than by symbols.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_38g3: Pressed for the Luftschutz, the Gladiator style favored comfort and coverage in streets gone dark.Three joined sections shape the crown and skirt, paint laid matte so light would not catch on it.It remembers stairwells, torchlight, and the hush after sirens when neighbors counted the seconds together.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_38g2: A rarer two-piece shell, the crown and skirt joined cleanly with the Luftschutz badge sharp over the brow.A rear size mark sits neat above smooth paint.It carries the quiet work of its branch—doorways, stairwells, and the dust that settles after the all-clear.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_38g1: The scarce one-piece Gladiator shell, pressed in a single form and marked with the Luftschutz eagle at the brow.Light and rigid, it sits close to the head; the rear size stencil is crisp, the paint smooth to the touch.It recalls wardens moving through stairwells and courtyards, guiding voices in the dark.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_mp40: The MP40 was Germany’s standard submachine gun of the Second World War, chambered in 9×19mm Parabellum and fed from a 32-round magazine. Stamped steel parts and a folding stock made it practical for mass production and compact for paratroops, vehicle crews, and squad leaders. It fired at around 500 rounds per minute, controllable in bursts but intended for close combat rather than long-range precision. Allied troops often called it the “Schmeisser,” and later soldier slang gave it nicknames such as the “Ghetto Blaster.”
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_ammo_9x19_fmj: Known also as 9mm Luger, this cartridge was the standard pistol and submachine gun round of the German armed forces. The FMJ load, with its copper-jacketed lead core, fed reliably in automatic weapons from the Luger P08 and Walther P38 pistols to the MP38 and MP40 submachine guns. Its manageable recoil and high magazine capacity made it ideal for short- to medium-range engagements, though less powerful than rifle ammunition.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_mag_mp40_9x19mm: Detachable steel box magazine holding 32 rounds of 9×19mm Parabellum for the MP40. Compact and robust, it allowed German infantry to sustain bursts of automatic fire before reloading. Soldiers carried multiple loaded magazines in pouches; dents or fouling could cause stoppages, so keeping them clean was as important as having them full.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_mp38: The MP38 is an early German 9×19mm submachine gun that directly preceded the MP40. Featuring milled and pressed components with a folding stock, it provided controllable automatic fire from a 32-round box magazine. Slightly lighter on recoil than later variants, the MP38 was favored for close-quarters use, vehicle crews, and airborne troops.
infotexts.entitydescription.oh_mag_mp38_9x19mm: Detachable steel box magazine for the MP38, holding 32 rounds of 9×19mm Parabellum. Interchangeable with the later MP40, it uses a double-column, single-feed design: reliable when clean, but sensitive to dents and fouling. Issued in pairs in belt pouches and commonly filled with a clip-on loading tool, it enabled fast magazine swaps for sustained close-quarters fire.
